edit_from_base: 'uses a normal map so they react to the 2D lights' -> 'scrolls by shifting the UV over time'
prompt: Give the ground tiles a material that scrolls by shifting the UV over time.

config.plan_model: Agent-tool model parameter 'sonnet' (Claude Code sub-agent; the harness did not report the resolved model id)
config.how: one fresh general-purpose sub-agent per plan, reads a job file with project brief + the developer prompt, writes numbered plan (<=8 steps, no code) via Write; not Claude Code plan mode

plans.text:
1. Open the TileMapLayer node in level_01.tscn and note which tile set and atlas the ground tiles use, so the material is applied only to the ground and not to platforms or other layers if they share a layer.
2. Decide whether the ground and platforms live on the same TileMapLayer; if they do, split the ground into its own TileMapLayer so the scrolling material affects only the ground.
3. Create a new canvas_item shader file (for example ground_scroll.gdshader) in the project's shaders or assets folder.
4. In the shader, offset the UV by a time-based amount along the chosen axis, expose scroll speed and direction as uniform parameters, and make sure the texture repeats (or that the tile atlas is sampled safely) so edges do not bleed into neighboring tiles.
5. Create a ShaderMaterial resource that uses this shader and assign it to the ground TileMapLayer's Material property in the inspector.
6. Check the tile atlas texture's filter and repeat import settings, since scrolling UVs across an atlas can pull in pixels from adjacent tiles, and adjust the shader to clamp the shifted UV within each tile's region if needed.
7. Run level_01.tscn and verify the ground visibly scrolls at a sensible speed, the Player's collision and the two enemy scenes are unaffected, and no seams or flicker appear.
8. Tune the speed uniform values and save the material as a reusable resource so other levels can use it.

1. Open the TileMapLayer node for the ground and platforms in level_01.tscn and confirm which tileset and tile layer the ground tiles live on, so the effect targets only those tiles.
2. Decide how to scope the effect: a CanvasItem shader material applies to the whole TileMapLayer, so check whether platforms share the same layer and, if they must stay static, move ground tiles to their own TileMapLayer.
3. Create a new canvas_item shader resource for the scrolling ground, with a speed parameter exposed as a uniform so the scroll direction and rate can be tuned in the inspector.
4. In the shader, offset the UV by the time value multiplied by the speed, and make sure the tile texture or atlas wraps cleanly so the shift does not bleed into neighboring atlas tiles.
5. Because the tiles come from a shared atlas, handle the atlas bounds: either wrap the UV within each tile's region or give the ground tiles a separate texture with repeat enabled.
6. Create a ShaderMaterial, assign the new shader, and attach it to the ground TileMapLayer's material property.
7. Run level_01.tscn and check that the ground scrolls smoothly, tile seams look right, and the Player's collision and movement on the ground are unaffected, since only visuals changed.
8. Tune the speed value and check the other levels or enemy scenes that reuse the tileset for unintended scrolling, then save the scene and shader.

1. Open the TileMapLayer node in level_01.tscn and check how the ground tiles are currently set up (tileset, atlas texture, any existing material), so the change targets only the ground and not the platforms or enemies.
2. Decide which layer carries the ground tiles; if ground and platforms share one TileMapLayer, split the ground into its own TileMapLayer so a material can be applied to it alone.
3. Create a new shader resource (canvas_item type) that offsets the UV by a time-based amount along the chosen scroll axis, with exposed parameters for scroll speed and direction.
4. Create a ShaderMaterial resource that uses this shader and save it as a reusable file in the project's materials or shaders folder.
5. Assign the ShaderMaterial to the ground TileMapLayer's Material property in the Inspector.
6. Check the tileset atlas texture's import settings, and make sure its repeat mode allows wrapping so the shifted UVs tile seamlessly instead of clamping or showing edge bleed.
7. Run level_01 and verify the ground scrolls at a sensible speed and direction, that tile seams and borders look correct, and that player collisions and enemies are unaffected.
8. Tune the speed parameter, and confirm other levels or the TileMapLayer's platforms are not unintentionally affected; save the scene.

1. Inspect the TileMapLayer's current setup (tile set, atlas texture, tile size, any existing material) to confirm how ground tiles are drawn and which tiles count as "ground" versus platforms.
2. Decide the scope: apply the effect to the whole ground TileMapLayer if ground and platforms are on separate layers, or split ground into its own TileMapLayer so only ground tiles scroll.
3. Create a new canvas_item shader (a .gdshader file) in a shaders folder, designed to offset the UV by a time-driven amount.
4. Expose shader parameters for scroll speed and direction so the developer can tune the effect in the Inspector without editing the shader.
5. Make the texture sample repeat so scrolled UVs wrap seamlessly, and check how the atlas is laid out, since shifting UVs across an atlas can bleed into neighboring tiles and may need per-tile UV clamping or a dedicated texture.
6. Create a ShaderMaterial resource that uses the shader and assign it to the ground TileMapLayer's Material property (or to the tile's material in the TileSet).
7. Run level_01.tscn and confirm the ground visibly scrolls, that collisions and the Player's movement are unaffected, and that the platforms and enemies look unchanged.
8. Tune speed, direction, and wrap behavior, then save the scene and material so the setup persists.

1. Open the TileMapLayer node in level_01.tscn and inspect its TileSet to confirm which tiles are the ground and platform tiles and whether ground tiles share a single atlas source. Check whether platforms should scroll too or only the ground.
2. Decide how the scroll will be applied: a canvas_item ShaderMaterial on the TileMapLayer is simplest, but it affects every tile on that layer. If only ground should scroll, move ground to its own TileMapLayer or use per-tile custom data to mask it.
3. Create a new canvas_item shader resource that offsets the UV by a time-based amount, with exposed uniforms for scroll direction and speed. Make sure the texture repeat mode is set so shifted UVs wrap instead of clamping.
4. Handle atlas pitfalls: since a TileSet atlas packs many tiles into one texture, shifting the UV across the whole atlas would bleed neighboring tiles into view. Constrain the shift to each tile's region, or use a separate texture for the ground tiles.
5. Create a ShaderMaterial, assign the shader to it, and set it as the material on the ground TileMapLayer (or on the ground tile's material in the TileSet). Tune the speed and direction uniforms in the inspector.
6. Run level_01.tscn and verify the ground visibly scrolls smoothly, with no seams or flicker at tile borders. Confirm the Player's CollisionShape2D and physics are unaffected, since a shader only changes visuals.
7. Check that the Player sprite, enemies, and platforms (if excluded) render normally and that nothing else inherited the material. Test at different window sizes and zoom levels for pixel snapping artifacts.
8. Save the shader and scene changes, and note the uniform names and intended usage so the speed can be reused or tweaked on other levels.

1. Inspect the TileMapLayer node in level_01.tscn and its TileSet to identify which tiles count as ground, and check whether ground and platforms share one layer or atlas source. This decides whether the effect can be applied to the whole layer or needs a separate layer.
2. Decide the scope: scroll only the ground tiles, not platforms or other tiles. If they share a layer, split the ground into its own TileMapLayer so the material affects only it.
3. Create a new CanvasItem shader (spatial shaders do not apply to 2D) that offsets the UV by a speed uniform multiplied by TIME. Expose scroll speed and direction as uniforms, and wrap or repeat the sampling so the texture tiles seamlessly.
4. Account for the tile atlas: shifting UV across a whole atlas texture will bleed into neighboring tiles. Either use the tile's own region bounds to wrap the offset within each tile, or make the ground a separate texture so the shift stays inside it.
5. Create a ShaderMaterial that uses this shader and assign it to the ground TileMapLayer's Material property (CanvasItem section). Set sensible default speed values.
6. Confirm that the ground tile texture has its repeat mode enabled (or is otherwise import-configured) so shifted UVs wrap instead of clamping to a stretched edge.
7. Run level_01.tscn and verify the ground scrolls smoothly, platforms and enemies are unaffected, and Player collision and movement in player.gd still behave correctly, since the shader changes visuals only.
8. Tune the speed and direction uniforms by eye, then save the material as a reusable resource so other levels can use it.

1. Open level_01.tscn and the TileMapLayer node to confirm how the ground tiles are set up (tile set, texture atlas, tile size) and which tiles count as ground versus platforms.
2. Decide the scope: apply the scrolling material to the ground tiles only, either through a separate TileMapLayer for ground or through the tile set's per-tile material setting, so platforms stay unaffected.
3. Check the ground texture's import settings and the tile set's texture region setup, since UV shifting needs the texture to repeat and atlas tiles can bleed into neighbors when shifted.
4. Create a new canvas item shader resource for the scrolling effect, with a scroll speed parameter and a direction parameter, that offsets the UV by time and wraps within the tile's own region.
5. Create a ShaderMaterial that uses this shader and assign it to the ground TileMapLayer (or to the ground tiles), keeping the shader as a reusable resource file so other levels can share it.
6. Run level_01.tscn and check that the ground scrolls smoothly, tiles do not show seams or bleed from neighboring atlas tiles, and the Player's collision and movement in player.gd are unchanged.
7. Tune the speed and direction parameters in the inspector until the motion looks right, and confirm the platforms and both enemy scenes still render normally.
8. Check performance and the other levels or scenes that use the same tile set, then summarize the changes and any caveats for the developer.

1. Check how the TileMapLayer is currently set up (its TileSet, tile size, and whether it already has a material) and confirm which tile layer holds the ground tiles versus platforms. Note the texture atlas the ground tiles use, since scrolling the UV will sample that texture.
2. Decide the scroll behavior: direction, speed, and whether it should be an exposed, tweakable parameter. Also decide if the scroll should be limited to ground tiles only, so platforms and other tiles stay static.
3. Create a new canvas_item shader resource that offsets the UV by a speed value multiplied by elapsed time, wrapping the result so the texture repeats. Expose the speed as a uniform so it can be tuned from the Inspector.
4. Handle the atlas problem: shifting UV across a tile atlas will bleed into neighboring tiles, so the shader must wrap the offset within each tile's own region (or the ground tiles must use a separate, repeat-enabled texture). Pick whichever approach fits the existing art.
5. Create a ShaderMaterial using that shader and assign it to the ground tiles, either on the TileMapLayer's material property if the ground has its own layer, or per tile via the TileSet's material setting if ground and platforms share a layer.
6. Open level_01.tscn and run it to check the ground scrolls smoothly, tile seams line up, and the Player's collision and movement are unaffected, since this change is purely visual.
7. Tune the speed and direction values, and confirm the other scenes that use the same TileSet (including the two enemy scenes' levels, if any) look correct and no unintended tiles are animating.
8. Save the shader and material as reusable resources in the project, and mention any assumptions, such as tile atlas layout, to the developer.

1. Open level_01.tscn and inspect the TileMapLayer and its TileSet to confirm which layer and tiles count as ground, and check how the tile atlas texture is set up (size, filtering, repeat mode).
2. Decide the scroll approach: a canvas_item shader on the TileMapLayer that offsets the UV by a time-driven amount, with the texture repeat enabled so the shifted UV wraps cleanly instead of clamping.
3. Create a new shader resource (for example ground_scroll.gdshader) in the project's shaders or assets folder, with exposed uniforms for scroll speed and direction so the developer can tune it without editing the shader.
4. Create a ShaderMaterial that uses this shader, and save it as its own resource file so it can be reused and tweaked in the inspector.
5. Assign the material to the ground TileMapLayer, taking care that it affects only the ground tiles and not the platforms if those live on a separate layer (split them if needed), and check that the Player and enemies stay unaffected.
6. Watch for tile-atlas pitfalls: because UV shifting samples across the whole atlas, scrolling can bleed into neighboring tiles, so either restrict the shift to each tile's region or use per-tile textures, and set texture filter to nearest to keep pixels crisp.
7. Run level_01.tscn and verify the ground scrolls smoothly, loops without seams, does not interfere with collisions, and looks right at different speeds and resolutions.
8. Tune the default speed and direction to fit the level's feel, then summarize the change to the developer and commit the new shader and material files along with the updated scene.

1. Inspect how the TileMapLayer and its TileSet are currently set up in level_01.tscn, including which tiles are ground and whether any material is already assigned. Confirm the ground tiles share one atlas texture so a single material can cover them.
2. Decide the scope: apply the scrolling material only to the ground tiles, not the platforms or other layers. If ground and platforms share a layer, consider moving ground to its own TileMapLayer so the material affects only it.
3. Create a new canvas_item shader (a .gdshader file) that offsets the UV by a speed value multiplied by TIME. Expose the scroll speed and direction as uniforms so they can be tuned in the editor.
4. Check the tile texture's import and repeat settings so that shifted UVs wrap seamlessly instead of clamping or showing edge bleed. Also consider tile atlas bounds, since shifting UVs across an atlas can bleed into neighboring tiles and may need per-tile UV clamping or a dedicated texture.
5. Create a ShaderMaterial resource that uses the new shader, and assign it to the ground TileMapLayer's material property in level_01.tscn.
6. Run level_01 and visually verify that the ground scrolls smoothly in the intended direction. Tune the speed and check for seams, flicker, or tile-edge artifacts.
7. Confirm that the Player's collision and movement on the ground are unaffected, since the shader only changes visuals. Also check that the enemy scenes and platforms still render normally.
8. Save the shader and material in a sensible assets folder, and note the tunable uniforms for the developer.
